intros.market: Five CAs control 91% of publicly trusted certificate issuance, led by Let's Encrypt (37%) and Google Trust Services (21%). The market HHI of 2,240 indicates moderate concentration, with 89 trusted CAs but only 14 carrying meaningful volume. The remaining 75 CAs in the long tail collectively represent less than 9% of issuance yet maintain full trust store inclusion across browser platforms.
intros.trust: 335 trusted roots span four major trust stores, but only 90 roots appear in all four programs simultaneously. Microsoft maintains 142 roots not present in Chrome, Mozilla, or Apple, creating the largest source of cross-platform disagreement. Just 38 CA owners hold roots in all four stores, while store-specific inclusion creates operational complexity where a certificate chain validates in Edge but fails in Chrome or Safari.
intros.conc: The top three CAs issue 74% of all certificates, creating systemic dependency on Let's Encrypt, Google, and DigiCert. An outage or compromise at any of these operators would affect three-quarters of HTTPS connections globally. This concentration amplifies the impact of the 1,586 recorded incidents, as failures at dominant CAs cascade across a larger fraction of the encrypted web.
intros.tail: 75 CAs each hold less than 1% market share yet maintain full trust store inclusion, creating asymmetric risk exposure for browser vendors. These low-volume operators collectively generated 509 governance incidents and 338 revocation failures while serving a tiny fraction of users. The tail contains 30 government-operated CAs and multiple entries from high-risk jurisdictions, all with equal technical authority to issue for any domain.
intros.geo: U.S.-incorporated CAs issue 92% of all publicly trusted certificates despite representing only 15 of the 89 trusted authorities. Europe hosts 44 CAs contributing just 7% of issuance, while 17 Asia-Pacific CAs account for 0.1%. This geographic concentration means American corporate and legal jurisdiction governs the vast majority of global HTTPS traffic, independent of where certificates are actually deployed.
intros.gov: 30 government-operated or state-owned CAs hold trusted roots despite issuing only 0.08% of certificates. These entities span multiple regions including China, Russia, and several European nations flagged under jurisdiction risk frameworks. Their presence in trust stores grants sovereign actors the technical capability to issue certificates for any domain, regardless of actual issuance volume.
intros.jurisdiction: Five jurisdictions are classified as high-risk for compelled disclosure or surveillance: China, Russia, the United Kingdom, Australia, and Hong Kong. India and Turkey carry moderate risk designations. CAs incorporated in these regions face legal frameworks that may compel assistance in surveillance or certificate issuance, creating potential conflicts with baseline requirements and user expectations of certificate integrity.
intros.ops: 1,586 incidents across 54 CAs reveal systemic compliance failures, led by 614 misissuances and 509 governance breakdowns. Only 27% of incidents are self-detected, while 199 cases involved explicit policy violations and 139 reflect disclosure failures. External researchers and automated tools discover more problems than CAs find internally, indicating weak internal controls despite annual audits and root program oversight.
intros.crypto: Root algorithm diversity and key size compliance form the technical foundation of trust store security. The cryptographic posture data encompasses signature algorithms, key lengths, and adherence to NIST and CA/Browser Forum standards. Transitions from SHA-1 and 1024-bit RSA to SHA-256 and 2048-bit minimum key sizes reflect multi-year ecosystem upgrades coordinated across root programs.
intros.distrust: 16 distrust events have removed CA access to browser trust stores, with 14 cases citing compliance or operational failures. 10 events followed a pattern of repeated issues rather than single incidents. Posture analysis shows 7 cases of negligent noncompliance and 3 of demonstrated incompetence, with CAs receiving a median 1,185 days to wind down operations before final removal.
intros.policy: Active TLS-issuing CAs face cascading validity limits under SC-081: 200 days in March 2026, 100 days in March 2027, and 47 days by March 2029. Among 36 measured CAs, 3 remain at risk for the 200-day threshold and 5 for the 100-day limit, while only 8 have reached 47-day operational readiness with a median of 68 days. These technical migrations occur against a compliance surface that has grown 121x since 2000 to 6,657 total obligations spanning CA/B Forum baseline requirements, four root program policies, WebTrust and ETSI audit criteria, and ISO/NIST standards, with 76% carrying mandatory enforcement and zero simplification ballots passed since 2022.
intros.governance: Root program oversight coverage has collapsed from 68-78% in 2019 to 18% in 2025 for Chrome and 10% for Mozilla across 223 incidents. Apple provides substantive comment on just 5% of cases, while Microsoft maintains zero participation in public incident review. Chrome has engaged with 732 total oversight bugs but only 112 recent substantive comments, indicating declining engagement even as incident volume remains steady.
intros.community: 56 organizations hold CA/Browser Forum membership, but only 21 actively participate and 35 contribute zero ballot activity. Sectigo leads organizational participation while Stephen Davidson has proposed 36 ballots individually. This concentration leaves governance dependent on a small active minority while the silent majority benefits from trust store inclusion without contributing to standards development.
intros.audit: Auditors detected just 34% of incidents that occurred during their in-scope review periods, with 146 findings from 425 incidents covered by active audit engagements. 39 CAs show high transparency gaps between clean audit opinions and public incident records, while 5 received qualified opinions. 59% of WebTrust letters and 67% of ETSI reports were self-submitted rather than program-verified, enabling selective disclosure. 11 CAs changed auditors in 2025 and only 10 have adopted ETSI EN 319 411-1 v3.5, the latest standard, indicating audit rigor lags behind the operational reality visible in the 1,586-incident corpus.
